title: The training principles series： overtraining
summary: His take on overtraining. It exists but is individual, and it shrinks as you get better, so a natural lifter should aim to become 'unovertrainable'. It is mostly a problem for eager beginners, and 'under-recovered' is a better term. Body part splits let you track how fatigued each muscle is so you can train right up to the edge without going over.

claims.claim: Overtraining, the idea that training too much causes injury and no progress, is real.
Overtraining is subjective and individual: what overtrains one person may not overtrain another.
The more advanced you get, the less overtraining is possible.
A natural lifter should aim to become 'unovertrainable': muscles so strong and resilient that no amount of work makes you sick, injured or regress.
An advanced natural lifter will usually burn out mentally or get bored before the body reaches overtraining.
Overtraining is a real issue for very motivated beginners: just 2-3 extra sets can burn them out for a while, though rarely anything more serious.
Rhabdomyolysis mostly happens with intense cardio or when a coach forces you to finish reps; training alone you'd get injured before getting rhabdo.

'Under-rested' or 'under-recovered' is a better term: overtraining within one session is nearly impossible with some experience, but you can train too much and come back to the next session not fully recovered.
Showing up under-recovered means wasted training, injury risk or not performing at your best.
Body part splits solve under-recovery because they let you give each muscle a known level of fatigue per session, so you know how recovered it is next time.
He always knows the recovery state of every body part because he knows what each session does to his body; this comes from experience programming for yourself.
Once you understand overtraining you can use it: train right below the edge of overtraining so you work your muscles to the max and maximize hypertrophy.
